items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from climatic variations and human activities (UN definition)”.
items.answer: Desertification
items.markingKey: Desertification: land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from climatic variations and human activities (UN definition). [1]

items.stem: Explain the human causes of desertification.
items.answer: Overgrazing, overcultivation and shorter fallows, deforestation for fuelwood, poor irrigation causing salinisation, population growth, sedentarisation and cash-crop expansion onto marginal land.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per cause [4]

items.stem: Explain the impacts of desertification on people.
items.answer: Falling crop yields and loss of pasture; food insecurity and malnutrition; loss of income; migration to cities; conflict over land and water; dust storms affecting health.

items.stem: A grazing area in Darfur, Sudan covers 8 000 ha. Grass production averages 1500 kg of dry matter per hectare per year, of which only 40% can be eaten without damaging the pasture. One tropical livestock unit (TLU) eats about 2 300 kg of dry matter a year. The present herd is 2 525 TLU. Calculate the carrying capacity of the area in TLU.
items.answer: 2 087 TLU

items.stem: A grazing area in Darfur, Sudan covers 5 000 ha. Grass production averages 1500 kg of dry matter per hectare per year, of which only 50% can be eaten without damaging the pasture. One tropical livestock unit (TLU) eats about 2 300 kg of dry matter a year. The present herd is 1 580 TLU. (a) Calculate the carrying capacity of the area in TLU. (b) Suggest why carrying capacity in a drought year would be lower.
items.answer: (a) 1 630 TLU (b) Less rain means less grass growth, so the same herd exceeds the capacity; animals concentrate around remaining water.

items.stem: A communal grazing area in Botswana covers 12 000 ha. Grass production averages 1500 kg of dry matter per hectare per year, of which only 50% can be eaten without damaging the pasture. One tropical livestock unit (TLU) eats about 2 300 kg of dry matter a year. The present herd is 6 419 TLU. (a) Calculate the present stocking as a percentage of carrying capacity and state whether the area is overgrazed. (b) Suggest why carrying capacity in a drought year would be lower.
items.answer: (a) 164%: overgrazed (b) Less rain means less grass growth, so the same herd exceeds the capacity; animals concentrate around remaining water.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that desertification is caused more by human activity than by climate? In your answer you may refer to drought, recovery and population.
items.answer: For: Overgrazing, overcultivation, deforestation and poor irrigation directly degrade land; the UN definition stresses human activities. Against: Drought and climatic variability (Sahel 1970s-80s) drive many degradation episodes; vegetation recovered when rains returned; climate change increases aridity. Conclusion: Climate triggers degradation, but human pressures turn drought into lasting desertification.

options: A person forced to leave their home because of environmental change such as drought or desertification.
Land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from climatic variations and human activities (UN definition).
A shortage of wood for cooking and heating, which leads to clearance of trees and shrubs.
A reduction in the biological or economic productivity of land.

items.stem: A student writes: “Desertification means that deserts are steadily advancing.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It is patchy degradation, often around settlements and water points, not an advancing front.

items.stem: Explain the role of feedback in desertification.
items.answer: Loss of vegetation increases albedo and reduces evapotranspiration and moisture recycling, which may reduce rainfall, causing more vegetation loss (Charney hypothesis).

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a low-cost technique in which farmers protect and prune tree stumps and shoots regrowing in their fields”.
items.answer: Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR)

items.stem: Explain why FMNR is considered sustainable.
items.answer: It is cheap and uses existing root stocks; farmers own the trees and benefit from fuel, fodder and fruit; trees reduce wind erosion and improve soil fertility; spreads farmer to farmer.

items.stem: Explain why large tree-planting schemes in drylands often fail.
items.answer: Seedlings die without water and care; species unsuited to local conditions; little local ownership; grazing animals eat seedlings; insecurity and funding gaps.

items.answer: Stone lines, zaï pits and half-moons slow run-off, increase infiltration, trap sediment and organic matter, raise yields and allow trees and grasses to regenerate.

items.stem: “Small-scale local schemes are more successful than large-scale projects in managing arid areas sustainably.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: FMNR and zaï pits in Niger and Burkina Faso are cheap, owned by farmers and have regreened millions of hectares. Against: Large projects such as the Loess Plateau scheme achieved major improvements with government and World Bank funding; national policy (tree tenure laws) enabled local success; the Great Green Wall shows large schemes can fail without local ownership. Conclusion: Local ownership is the key to success; large-scale schemes work when they support local action rather than impose top-down solutions.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “groundwater stored in aquifers thousands of years ago and not being recharged under the present climate”.

items.stem: Explain why the use of fossil water is unsustainable.
items.answer: Aquifers are not recharged under present climates, so extraction lowers the water table permanently; wells must go deeper and costs rise; supplies will eventually run out.

items.stem: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of drip irrigation.
items.answer: Advantages: efficiency up to 90-95%, less salinisation, fertiliser applied with water, higher yields. Disadvantages: high installation cost, clogging, needs maintenance and reliable water pressure, less suited to some crops.

A farmer at a farm in Arizona, USA grows 50 ha of cotton, which needs 700 mm of water per season. 1 mm of water over 1 ha = 10 m³. Irrigation efficiencies: flood 45%, sprinkler 70%, drip 85%. (a) Calculate the crop water requirement for the farm in m³. (b) Explain why flood irrigation is inefficient in hot arid climates.
items.answer: (a) 350 000 m³ (b) High evaporation from open channels and wet soil; seepage from unlined canals; water percolates below the roots; run-off from the field.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that technology can solve water shortages in arid environments. In your answer you may refer to governance and desalination.
items.answer: For: Desalination (Israel, the Gulf states), drip irrigation, water recycling and pipelines (Great Man-Made River) have greatly increased supply. Against: Technology is costly and energy-intensive; fossil aquifers will run out; demand management, pricing, governance and traditional methods are needed; conflicts over shared rivers (Nile, Tigris-Euphrates). Conclusion: Technology helps, but sustainable water management depends on reducing demand and fair governance.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a person forced to leave their home because of environmental change such as drought or desertification”.
items.answer: Environmental refugee
items.markingKey: Environmental refugee: a person forced to leave their home because of environmental change such as drought or desertification. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the role of feedback in desertification. (b) A revision website states: “Population growth always causes desertification.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Loss of vegetation increases albedo and reduces evapotranspiration and moisture recycling, which may reduce rainfall, causing more vegetation loss (Charney hypothesis). (b) Not correct. In Machakos, Kenya, more people led to better land management ("More people, less erosion").
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Desertification can be reversed.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the human causes of desertification.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Regreening in Niger and Burkina Faso shows land can recover. (b) Overgrazing, overcultivation and shorter fallows, deforestation for fuelwood, poor irrigation causing salinisation, population growth, sedentarisation and cash-crop expansion onto marginal land.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark per cause [4]

items.stem: A pastoral area in northern Burkina Faso covers 5 000 ha. Grass production averages 600 kg of dry matter per hectare per year, of which only 50% can be eaten without damaging the pasture. One tropical livestock unit (TLU) eats about 2 300 kg of dry matter a year. The present herd is 779 TLU. Suggest why carrying capacity in a drought year would be lower.
items.answer: Less rain means less grass growth, so the same herd exceeds the capacity; animals concentrate around remaining water.

items.stem: A grazing area in Darfur, Sudan covers 12 000 ha. Grass production averages 600 kg of dry matter per hectare per year, of which only 40% can be eaten without damaging the pasture. Calculate the present stocking as a percentage of carrying capacity and state whether the area is overgrazed.
items.answer: 115.2%: overgrazed

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that desertification is caused more by human activity than by climate? In your answer you may refer to overgrazing and population.
items.answer: For: Overgrazing, overcultivation, deforestation and poor irrigation directly degrade land; the UN definition stresses human activities. Against: Drought and climatic variability (Sahel 1970s-80s) drive many degradation episodes; vegetation recovered when rains returned; climate change increases aridity. Conclusion: Climate triggers degradation, but human pressures turn drought into lasting desertification.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A revision website states: “The Loess Plateau project reduced sediment loads in the Yellow River.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why large tree-planting schemes in drylands often fail.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Terracing and vegetation sharply reduced erosion. (b) Seedlings die without water and care; species unsuited to local conditions; little local ownership; grazing animals eat seedlings; insecurity and funding gaps.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [3]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why FMNR is considered sustainable. (b) Explain how water harvesting techniques help to combat desertification.
items.answer: (a) It is cheap and uses existing root stocks; farmers own the trees and benefit from fuel, fodder and fruit; trees reduce wind erosion and improve soil fertility; spreads farmer to farmer. (b) Stone lines, zaï pits and half-moons slow run-off, increase infiltration, trap sediment and organic matter, raise yields and allow trees and grasses to regenerate.

items.stem: Using one named example of the sustainable management of an arid or semi-arid area, describe the strategies used to manage the area.
items.answer: the Loess Plateau, China: Loess Plateau Watershed Rehabilitation Project (1994-2005, World Bank) and Grain for Green: terraces, check dams, bans on free grazing, tree and grass planting on steep slopes, land tenure for farmers.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “drip irrigation”?
options: Delivering water slowly to plant roots through pipes and emitters, reducing evaporation losses.
The percentage of water applied that is actually used by the crop.
Removing salt from seawater or brackish water to make it usable.
A traditional gently sloping underground channel that carries groundwater from hills to settlements by gravity.
items.answer: Delivering water slowly to plant roots through pipes and emitters, reducing evaporation losses.

items.stem: A revision website states: “Irrigation always increases food security in the long term.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Salinisation and aquifer depletion can reduce production over time.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the use of fossil water is unsustainable. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Desalination has no environmental costs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Aquifers are not recharged under present climates, so extraction lowers the water table permanently; wells must go deeper and costs rise; supplies will eventually run out. (b) Not correct. It uses much energy and discharges concentrated brine.

items.stem: A farmer at a farm near Ouarzazate, Morocco grows 120 ha of cotton, which needs 700 mm of water per season. 1 mm of water over 1 ha = 10 m³. Irrigation efficiencies: flood 40%, sprinkler 75%, drip 85%. Suggest why many farmers in LICs still use flood irrigation.
items.answer: Low cost and simple technology; drip systems are expensive and need maintenance, filters and pumps; water is cheap or unpriced; small, fragmented plots.

items.stem: A farmer at a farm near Ouarzazate, Morocco grows 25 ha of alfalfa, which needs 1200 mm of water per season. 1 mm of water over 1 ha = 10 m³. Irrigation efficiencies: flood 40%, sprinkler 75%, drip 85%. (a) Calculate the crop water requirement for the farm in m³. (b) Explain why flood irrigation is inefficient in hot arid climates.
items.answer: (a) 300 000 m³ (b) High evaporation from open channels and wet soil; seepage from unlined canals; water percolates below the roots; run-off from the field.
